function_question: How does nature build strong structures from little material?

opening.text: There was a girl called Nia, 15, who ran her school's engineering club and kept the glue far away from her little brother Kofi.
Nia sketched bridges on everything: napkins, notebooks, even the back of Kofi's homework.

An engineering competition was announced. "The prize goes to the bridge that holds the most per gram," Nia read. Kofi held up a bridge wrapped in a whole roll of tape. "Strong!" he said. "And heavy," Nia sighed.

card.problem: The prize is for most weight held per gram
card.rules: Span 30 cm with paper, card and sticks

guide.brief: I'm Popi, your story guide. Nia's competition bridge must hold the most weight for every gram it weighs, and Kofi's tape-covered version is far too heavy. Can you help her? Let's start!
guide.your_idea: Some engineers already picture a light, strong shape. Do you?
guide.nature_clues: Nature builds strong things out of almost nothing. Tap each card to meet four lightweight champions!
guide.design_secret: Here's the secret all four heroes share…
guide.skill: Same sheet, different shape. Which paper beam will hold the most coins? Predict first, then test!
guide.sketch: Draw your bridge with arrows: which parts get squashed, and which get pulled?
guide.build_and_test: Weigh your bridge, load it until it fails, then divide. What's your efficiency score?
guide.retry_tip: Find where it broke first. Strengthen that spot, remove material where nothing broke, and test again!
guide.ending: And ever since then, Nia's club builds everything the nature way, and Kofi proudly uses just a little tape!

quick_check.question: Bridge A weighs 25 g and holds 1,500 g. Bridge B weighs 40 g and holds 2,000 g. Which has the better efficiency score?
quick_check.right: Right! 1,500 ÷ 25 = 60 and 2,000 ÷ 40 = 50. Bridge B holds more, but Bridge A wins per gram!
quick_check.wrong: Not quite. Divide each load by the bridge's own weight, then compare.

clue_cards.name: Bird bone
clue_cards.trick: Its hollow wing bones have thin criss-cross struts inside.
clue_cards.does: The struts form triangles, so the bones are strong but light enough for flight.

clue_cards.name: Bone trabeculae
clue_cards.trick: Tiny bone struts line up along the paths the forces take.
clue_cards.does: Bone adds material where it is loaded and removes it where it isn't.

clue_cards.name: Giant water lily
clue_cards.trick: A web of thick ribs spreads out under its thin leaf.
clue_cards.does: The ribs stiffen a leaf up to 3 metres wide, strong enough for a small child on a board.

clue_cards.name: Spider web
clue_cards.trick: Every thread is pulled tight, never squashed.
clue_cards.does: Gram for gram, its silk is stronger than steel, so a web needs very little material.

predict.explain: When a load pushes down on the middle of a beam, the beam bends. Its top edge gets squashed together and its bottom edge gets stretched. Webs and cables only ever work in tension.

lab.title: The paper beam lab
lab.predict: One sheet of A4 paper spans a 20 cm gap, folded into four different shapes. Which will hold the most coins?
